title: Eight Weeks Toward a Slower Temper
subtitle: An eight-week plan from James Bell for the temper that keeps winning. Where the line falls, what anger signals and defends, the time-out, repair, anger at God, and forgiveness that isn't silence.
intro:
This is an eight-week plan for you if your temper keeps winning: the shout at your children over something small, the slammed door, the words to your spouse you can't take back, then the shame, the apology, and a few days later the same fire. It's for anger that runs cold, too, and for anger aimed at God. Each week holds one focus, one small daily practice, one thing to read, one tool to use, and one honest question. It begins with where the line falls between a temper and abuse, then moves slowly through what your anger signals and defends, the body and the time-out, repair, anger at God, and forgiveness, toward a slower way of living. If someone else's anger frightens you, this plan was written for the one with the temper. Put your safety first, because keeping them calm was never your job. The Domestic Violence Hotline on the Find Help page is for you, and if you're under eighteen, tell a teacher, a school counselor, or another adult you trust, and call 911 if you're in danger.

This plan isn't a cure, and it isn't a substitute for a doctor, a licensed counselor, a pastor, or the real people who can help you change. If you're ever afraid of what you might do to a child, make sure the child is safe, step away, and call someone now: a friend, your doctor, or 988, where you don't have to be suicidal to call. Lay a baby on their back in the crib first, and never shake a baby. Walk the plan imperfectly. A missed week is not failure; you just pick it back up. Your check marks are saved only in this browser.
careNote: If your partner is afraid of you, or you've hit, shoved, threatened, or controlled them, call the Domestic Violence Hotline on Find Help and ask about an intervention program; if your children are afraid or your anger is constant, see a doctor or licensed counselor. In a crisis, or if you're afraid of what you might do, call or text 988, and 911 if anyone is in danger.

weeks.focus: Safety first, then the truth about your temper
weeks.why: Start with the hardest question, because everything after it depends on the answer: is anyone afraid of you? Anger isn't always a sin, and a temper can change. But hitting, shoving, choking, or threatening a partner, breaking things to frighten them, or using your temper to control where they go and whom they see is abuse, not a temper problem. Abuse is a pattern of power and control, and the help is built for that: the National Domestic Violence Hotline on Find Help, which also talks with people worried about their own behavior, and an intervention program for people who have harmed a partner. The Hotline doesn't recommend anger management or couples counseling for abuse. If it's your children who are afraid, make sure they're safe and see a doctor or counselor this week. A family that tiptoes around your moods is telling you something.
weeks.practice: Each day, write down one time anger rose: what set it off, what you did, and who saw it, with no excuses. If your partner is afraid of you, call the Hotline today; if your children are, a doctor or counselor. When you feel it rising, leave the room, and never block anyone from leaving. Don't press anyone you've frightened to forgive you or go to counseling with you. Call or text 988 if you're afraid of what you might do, and 911 if anyone is in danger.

tool.label: The Find Help page, where the Domestic Violence Hotline is listed with 988 and 911

weeks.reflection: Who in my home has learned to read my moods, and what have they been doing to keep me calm?

weeks.focus: A signal before it is a sin
weeks.why: Scripture doesn't call all anger sin. God is angry at evil, and Mark says Jesus looked at men who would rather a man's hand stay withered than see their Sabbath rules bent "with anger and sorrow at their hardness of heart" (Mark 3:5). His anger grieved, it was aimed at harm done to someone else, and it ended in healing; much of what we call righteous anger, mine included, fails those tests. Before it is ever a sin, anger is a signal. It flares where something matters to you, and it climbs before it explodes: heat in the face, a tight jaw, a rising voice, a sentence already forming about what they always do. The letter of James asks for slowness, "Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger" (James 1:19), and slowness starts with noticing the climb.
weeks.practice: Think back over your last few blowups. What did your body do first: heat in your face, a clenched jaw, a louder voice? What were you telling yourself? Had you slept, eaten, or been drinking? Write it down. Then each day, the moment you notice the first sign, say it out loud: I'm getting angry. This week's reading sends violent anger to a pastor and a counselor, but if your partner is afraid of you, the help starts with the Hotline and an intervention program, as in week one.

read.label: Is Anger a Sin? What Scripture Actually Says, on anger as information about what you love, the quick fuse and the slow one

tool.label: Psalm 4 in the Study Bible, the evening prayer the letter to the Ephesians quotes on anger, with a note on what its fourth verse means

weeks.reflection: What does my body do in the first seconds of anger, and what do I tell myself just before I blow up?

weeks.why: Fear says you're in danger and grief says you've lost something, but anger says someone was wrong. It hands down a verdict, which is why from the inside it feels like justice. Sometimes what it defends is good, a child who was mistreated or a wrong that's real. More often, if we're honest, it defends our pride, our comfort, and the expectation of being obeyed. The letter of James traces quarrels to their root: "You crave what you do not have... You quarrel and fight" (James 4:2). Underneath, anger often stands guard over what is harder to admit, like fear, hurt, shame, or grief, and some of us learned it at home, from a parent's temper or a parent's absence. Psalm 4, which bears David's name, gives the hour for asking: "on your bed, search your heart and be still" (Psalm 4:4).
weeks.practice: Each night before you sleep, do what Psalm 4 says: search your heart and be still. Ask what you wanted today and didn't get, whether respect, quiet, control, or your own way, and whether fear, grief, or shame sat underneath. Write one line. At the week's end, tell one honest person what you found, a friend, a pastor, or a counselor, and ask them to ask you again next week. If memories of being hurt come back with rage, panic, or nightmares, tell a doctor or counselor.

read.label: Anger: A Bible Study on Temper and Righteous Anger, session three, What Is Underneath the Anger

tool.label: How to Examine Your Day, ten minutes each night to look back over the day with God, failures included

weeks.reflection: When I'm angry, what am I usually afraid of losing, and is it something God loves or something I demand?

weeks.why: Anger is fast, and it lives in a body. Tiredness, hunger, pain, stress, and alcohol all shorten the fuse, and irritability that won't lift for weeks can be a sign of depression, which in men can look more like anger than sadness, so tell a doctor. Proverbs is blunt about drink: "Wine is a mocker, strong drink is a brawler" (Proverbs 20:1). Then build the pause before you need it. A time-out, agreed on while everyone is calm, is a word that means I'm too angry to talk well, I'm stepping away, and I'll be back. It's for cooling down, never for punishing anyone with silence. Don't spend it venting or rehearsing the argument, which turns out to feed anger rather than drain it: "A fool vents all his anger, but a wise man holds it back" (Proverbs 29:11).
weeks.practice: While everyone is calm, agree on a time-out word. When you use it, say when you'll be back, leave the room or walk, and return on time; don't drive. If you have a baby, lay them on their back in the crib first, and never shake a baby. Protect your sleep; eat before your worst hour. If you get angrier when you drink, stop this week; if you drink heavily every day, see a doctor first, because quitting suddenly can be dangerous.

read.label: How to Deal With Anger, on the pause between the spark and the words, and the different help a home afraid of you needs

tool.label: I can't stop drinking or using, the care page, with SAMHSA's helpline at the top, for when drinking feeds your temper

weeks.reflection: What state is my body usually in when I lose my temper, and what one change would take away the most fuel?

weeks.why: When your anger has hurt someone, the repair is yours to begin. Go back once you're calm and name what you did without a but: I yelled at you and said things that weren't true, and that was wrong; will you forgive me? Then say what you'll change, and change it, because an apology repeated without change becomes part of the pattern. Children need this as much as adults, and a parent who never says sorry teaches that the powerful never have to repent. If someone has something against you, Jesus said, leave your gift at the altar and "first go and be reconciled to your brother" (Matthew 5:24). But repair isn't getting what you want from the person you hurt. If they're afraid of you, don't press them to talk, to forgive you, or to go to counseling with you. Let changed behavior speak first.
weeks.practice: Choose one person your anger has hurt, a child, your spouse, a friend, a coworker, and when you're calm, go back. Name what you did with no but attached, say it was wrong, ask whether they'll forgive you, and tell them one thing you'll change. Accept the answer, even if it's not yet. If they're afraid of you, don't press for the conversation at all; let the change come first. Each night, settle the day's small wrongs before you sleep.

read.label: How to Apologize to Your Kids, on naming the wrong with no but attached, asking forgiveness, and then changing

tool.label: How to Repair After a Blowup, for couples who are safe with each other, on owning your part first and coming back when you said you would

weeks.reflection: Which apology have I made so many times without changing that it has stopped meaning anything, and what would the change look like?

weeks.focus: When the anger is at God
weeks.why: When anger is aimed at God, over a death or an unanswered prayer, faithful Christians differ on whether it's ever right. Some say never, because it accuses God of wrong, and he is "without injustice" (Deuteronomy 32:4). Bring him your grief and confusion, they say, and confess the anger itself, as Job did once God had spoken: "I retract my words, and I repent in dust and ashes" (Job 42:6). Their comfort is that God can be trusted even when he can't be understood. Others say anger brought to God can itself be a prayer, pointing to psalms that ask, "Why are You sleeping?" (Psalm 44:23), and to God's verdict that Job had spoken of him accurately (Job 42:7). Their comfort is that you don't have to clean yourself up to pray. The care page leaves both standing. Both agree: say it to God rather than walk away from him.
weeks.practice: Each day, say to God in plain words what you've been carrying toward him, and bring the anger too, whether you offer it as a prayer or confess it as sin. Don't go quiet or walk away. Read Job 42:1-9 one day, where Job answers the questions God put to him, and Jonah 4 another, where God questions an angry prophet. If your anger has turned on yourself, or you've thought about ending your life, call or text 988 now.

read.label: Job 42 in the Study Bible, where Job repents in dust and ashes and God says Job spoke of him accurately, with notes

tool.label: Jonah 4 in the Study Bible, where an angry prophet argues with God and the book ends on God's question, with notes

weeks.reflection: What have I been saying about God to other people, or to no one, that I have never said to him?

weeks.focus: Forgiveness that isn't silence or trust
weeks.why: Some anger runs cold. It's the grudge kept for years against a parent, a former spouse, a friend, or someone in the church, rehearsed until it shapes your days. Some of it may be telling the truth, and the church has too often told wronged people that their anger was the sin; I'm a pastor, so I'm inside that failure. The letter to the Ephesians allows anger and sets a deadline on it: "Do not let the sun set upon your anger" (Ephesians 4:26). Paul tells the Romans, "Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God's wrath" (Romans 12:19). Forgiveness starts with handing that debt to God instead of collecting it yourself. It isn't forgetting, excusing, trusting again, letting them back in, or keeping quiet about abuse or a crime. If they could still hurt you or a child, safety comes first.
weeks.practice: Choose one debt you've been collecting. Write three words across a page, forgive, trust, contact, and under each write where you honestly are; you may be ready for one and nowhere near the others. When the replay starts, pray one sentence instead of rerunning the argument: This is yours, and I'm not collecting it tonight. Forgiving them doesn't require contacting them, and if a crime was committed, you're still free to report it.

read.label: I can't forgive them, the care page on what forgiveness is and isn't, with safety first

tool.label: The Emotional Health Self-Check, whose forgiveness questions ask about rehearsing an offense, keeping score, and forgiving without trusting again

weeks.reflection: Whose debt have I been collecting for years, and what have I been afraid forgiving would force me to do?

weeks.why: At Sinai the LORD proclaimed his name to Moses: "compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6). In Hebrew, slow to anger is literally long of nose, as if anger were heat rising in the face and patience a long breath before it comes. Proverbs ranks that breath above conquest: "He who is slow to anger is better than a warrior, and he who controls his temper is greater than one who captures a city" (Proverbs 16:32). A slower temper won't arrive by willpower, or by next week. The letter to the Galatians names patience and self-control among the fruit of the Spirit, and fruit ripens slowly, on a few kept practices among people who know the truth about you. You have been living inside God's long breath for years, and the people at your table need a little of it from you.
weeks.practice: Write on a card the practices from these weeks that helped: your early warning signs, your time-out word, the nightly search of your heart, the apology with no but. Keep them daily. Ask one honest person, a friend, a pastor, or a counselor, to ask you each week how your temper has been, and tell them the truth. If anyone at home is still afraid of you, the card isn't enough; keep going with the program or counselor from week one.

read.label: Self-Control and Discipline, on a fruit of the Spirit grown slowly, small disciplines you can keep, and one person who hears your confession

tool.label: The Rule of Life Builder, to keep a few practices, one friend who knows the truth about you among them
